https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.title: Harrow’s Chinese outposts bow to Xi’s tyranny
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.text:
Harrow School has decided to open a new campus in China. The proposed educational facility in Guangzhou, which is set to receive about 1,500 students from Hong Kong, Macao and Taiwan in 2027, will be the ninth such campus Harrow runs in China.
Not surprisingly, human rights activists are appalled. The past few years have brought a Chinese curriculum clampdown and tougher controls on what is taught in classrooms. This year, Beijing introduced laws requiring all schools to have “patriotic education integrated into all subjects”. Schools must appoint up to five “assistant principals” to ensure children receive instruction in President Xi’s ideology and definition of the “rule of law”.
This makes nonsense of the claim made by Harrow’s international partner, Asia International School Limited (AISL) Harrow, that its schools in China “look to the 450-year old heritage of Harrow School in the UK to anchor its own guiding principles, drive progressive initiatives and inspire a vision that seeks to produce leaders for tomorrow”.
The repressive ideology and propaganda of the Chinese communist party are, one might confidently assume, diametrically opposed to the 450-year-old principles of Harrow School, or indeed any western school. That’s why Rugby School has chosen to open a branch in Japan after shunning offers from China that would restrict the curriculum and compromise Rugby’s core ethos. Other private schools have similarly chosen not to open Chinese outposts.
As Luke de Pulford, executive director of the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China, said: “Harrow’s China campus will be unable to criticise totalitarian [President] Xi, unable to call out the Uighur genocide, unable to teach whole swathes of history following the brainwashing diktats of the party-state. And for what?” For what indeed.
The issue of how far to engage with China has become an increasingly vexed one as the regime has tightened its tyrannical grip. This has presented an acute challenge in Hong Kong, where British judges sitting on the territory’s court of final appeal have wrestled for years over whether they would do more good by staying or leaving.
Contrary to China’s (always hollow) commitment to maintain an independent legal system with rights and freedoms in Hong Kong when Britain’s administration there ended in 1997, Beijing has progressively eroded the territory’s autonomy through a series of laws. In 2022, two British judges resigned from the Hong Kong court in protest at a Chinese law that curtailed freedom of speech and made it easier to punish protesters in Hong Kong. The other British judges decided to stay, saying they were satisfied with the court’s independence and that it was more important than ever to support Hong Kong in “maintaining the rule of law and reviewing the acts of the executive”.
At the time, it was a persuasive, if finely balanced, argument. However, as repression has subsequently grown even harsher, the balance has swung the other way. In May, Hong Kong’s pro-democracy media tycoon Jimmy Lai, who has been detained in December 2020 on national security charges and who was incarcerated for two years before his trial began, was separately convicted of “subversion”, along with a number of other pro-democracy activists, for participating in a peaceful protest in 2019.
For two of the remaining British judges, this was the last straw. Conscious of becoming increasingly sidelined as pawns of an oppressive legal system, Lord Sumption and Lord Collins of Mapesbury resigned. Sumption said Hong Kong was “slowly becoming a totalitarian state”; judges were being compromised by an “impossible political environment created by China”.
This has left three British judges who have chosen to remain on the court: Lord Hoffmann, Lord Neuberger of Abbotsbury and Lord Phillips of Worth Matravers. Neuberger, the former president of the UK’s supreme court, was one of the judges who last week unanimously dismissed the attempt by Lai and six other pro-democracy activists to overturn their convictions. Neuberger insisted his role was to decide cases that came before him according to the law. The court, he said, had “fully and impressively” considered the defendants’ fundamental human rights, including freedom of expression and assembly.
But what possible justification can it be to uphold the law when that law denies those rights and freedoms?
Like Harrow School, the three British judges who remain on the Hong Kong court are giving credibility and legitimacy to a tyrannical regime. Any possible benefits for Hong Kong defendants or pupils in China are now heavily outweighed by the damage these British participants are doing through undermining the astoundingly brave people desperately fighting the Chinese regime.
After the Cameron government so disastrously submitted to Beijing’s deadly embrace, British prime ministers have blown hot and cold over the UK’s institutionalised entanglement with a regime that poses such an acute threat to the West. Unlike the Conservatives, whose election manifesto pledged to declare China a security risk on a par with Russia and Iran, the Starmer government has declined to call China a “threat” and is pledging instead to co-operate with Beijing on health matters and “net zero”. As with Harrow and the three Hong Kong judicial stooges, kow-towing to the Chinese communist party is now apparently Labour’s “progressive” answer to tyranny.

https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.title: Morrisons’ freezers warm up to reduce emissions
https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.subtitle: Turning up dial by 3C will not affect food safety or quality, study finds
https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.text:
For almost a century, Britain’s households and food retailers have stored their fish fingers and peas in freezers set at -18°C, a temperature standard set in the 1930s. However, that may be about to change after Morrisons announced plans to become the first UK grocer to turn up the dial.
After research found that a higher setting would not affect food safety or quality, the supermarket chain said it planned to increase freezer temperatures to -15°C in ten of its stores in an effort to reduce costs, energy consumption and emissions.
“The standard temperature for the storage and transport of frozen food today looks like it is simply a convention from nearly 100 years ago,” Ruth McDonald, Morrisons’ corporate services director, said. “We now have vastly better freezers and modern technology and monitoring that gives us a precise picture of frozen food temperatures throughout the supply chain.”
The grocer is putting together a timetable to increase temperatures throughout its stores and frozen supply chain by 3C. “As we execute our plan, we will be encouraging our suppliers and partners to do the same,” McDonald said.
Food and logistics businesses have called for an increase in standard frozen temperatures. The metric was introduced to prevent bacterial growth and food-borne illnesses, but that was at a time when fewer studies and technologies were available. The Cold Chain Federation, the Global Cold Chain Alliance, DP World and MSC all want food to be stored and transported at –15C rather than -18C to save energy as the sector transitions to a net zero model.
A study from the Paris-based International Institute of Refrigeration, the University of Birmingham and London South Bank University found that raising the temperature by 3C could cut supply chain costs by between 5 per cent and 12 per cent. The study found that the change could save about 17.7 million tonnes of carbon dioxide per year, the equivalent emissions of 3.8 million cars annually, and would create energy savings of about 25 terawatt hours, roughly 8.6 per cent of the UK’s annual energy consumption.
A separate study by Nomad Foods, the frozen foods company behind Birds Eye and Findus, found that storing frozen food at –15C could reduce freezer energy consumption by more than 10 per cent without any noticeable impact on product safety, texture, taste or nutrition.
Stéfan Descheemaeker, the chief executive of Nomad Foods, said: “Increasing the temperature at which we store frozen food can significantly reduce energy consumption and carbon emissions. Establishing an end-to-end frozen industry alliance, to put our findings into action, will be the key to unlocking widespread change.”
Thomas Eskesen, chairman of the global Move to -15C Coalition, said that by raising the temperature of its freezers in ten stores, Morrisons was “demonstrating that change is possible and we know that this seemingly small change can lead to a significant, positive, environmental impact”.

image.caption: Morrisons, the supermarket chain, will encourage its suppliers to follow suit after it decided to change its freezer settingsALAMY

https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.title: Labour’s descent into sleaze was all too quick
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.text:
People might feel they’re having an acute episode of déjà vu all over again. When in opposition, the Labour Party was constantly banging on about kickbacks for Tory party donors and, in the words of Sir Keir Starmer, giving party supporters “dodgy contracts, jobs for their mates and cash for access”.Starmer promised to “restore standards in public life with a total crackdown on cronyism”. The hypocrisy is stunning. Almost every day recently has brought fresh revelations of Labour government cronyism and sleaze.
Lord Alli, a party fundraiser who donated £500,000 to Labour and made personal donations to Starmer, was given a Downing Street pass and last month hosted a post-election reception in No 10’s garden. It’s rare for anyone other than political advisers or civil servants to be given a Downing Street pass, or to host events at No 10. Alli is said to have given the pass back. Why he was given it in the first place remains a mystery.
Much more seriously, an apparently endless procession of Labour donors, supporters, activists and former party workers have been parachuted into government jobs that should have gone to impartial civil servants.
Ian Corfield, who gave £20,000 to the party, including £5,000 to the chancellor, Rachel Reeves, was given a job as the Treasury’s director of investment. Reeves reportedly didn’t inform senior Treasury officials of Corfield’s donation to her, an omission that appears to have broken the Ministerial Code.
Alarmed by the resulting furore over this, the government retreated. It emerged last weekend that Corfield would now be working as an unpaid adviser rather than a salaried civil servant. But that was far from all. Jess Sargeant, a constitutional reform expert from Labour Together, which gave hundreds of thousands of pounds to Labour candidates at the election, was appointed to a senior role at — of all things — the Cabinet Office’s propriety and constitution group, which is responsible for maintaining ethics across Whitehall.
Emily Middleton, another former Labour Together staffer who also worked for the current secretary of state for science and technology, Peter Kyle, when he was in opposition — with Middleton’s salary paid by her own private company as a donation in kind to Kyle — was appointed to a senior civil servant role in his science and technology department.
Henry Newman, a former Tory special adviser and author of The Whitehall Project blog, uncovered the fact that Ben Wood, who had worked for the Labour Party, and Rose Grayston, who was also previously employed at Labour Together, had been hired as civil servants in Angela Rayner’s housing department — along with another former Labour Party worker, Haydon Etherington.
These appointments and more cross the red lines that separate politics, government and business in order to guarantee the public interest in a clean civil service that works impartially for administrations of every stripe.
An early warning of Labour’s disdain for that public interest was sounded when Starmer, as leader of the opposition, poached Sue Gray — the former head of the same Cabinet Office ethics division — as his chief of staff. Although she observed a decompression period between working for the Cabinet Office and joining the Labour Party, there was criticism that she had compromised her impartiality as a civil servant by taking to the opposition the secrets of government.
Gray is reported to have been instrumental in these controversial civil service hirings. The government has tried to defend them on grounds of pragmatism, arguing that the best people had been appointed for the job.
This is highly disingenuous. It’s one thing appointing special advisers on grounds of their desirable expertise. It’s quite another to appoint political supporters or donors as civil servants, who are supposed to serve the public interest dispassionately rather than the interests of a party.
The government, however, seems to think that being Labour’s people and being the best people are one and the same thing.
Attempting to justify Alli’s Downing Street pass, the minister who runs the Cabinet Office, Pat McFadden, said: “But he does bring a huge amount to the Labour Party. He was an important part of the election campaign.”
The idea that there’s something unethical about a party donor being rewarded in this way was brushed aside as irrelevant. Labour ministers seem to believe their moral right to rule is so absolute that there’s no distinction between party and government.
This harks back to Sir Tony Blair’s comment in 1996 that the Labour Party was “the political arm” of the British people — a frightening attitude, because it justified an approach to government that casts political dissent as an offence against democracy.
Blair — who in similar vein said his aim was utterly to destroy the Conservative Party — made political appointees an integral part of government. William Gladstone’s achievement in creating in Whitehall the cleanest public administration institution in the world was unceremoniously dumped, along with much of the rest of Britain’s constitutional settlement.
People have long been sickened by the loss of integrity in political and public life. The resulting alienation is a profound threat to democracy.
Expectations of good things from the Starmer government were never high. But few can have expected that it would take less than two months for it to display such open and arrogant contempt for the ethical “high standards” it had pledged to uphold.

https://www.thetimes.com/world/ireland-w.title: U2 star Adam Clayton desires a cottage for his gardener at Danesmoate
https://www.thetimes.com/world/ireland-w.text:
Adam Clayton found what he was looking for when he was recording The Joshua Tree in 1986. A year later, he bought Danesmoate in Rathfarnham in Dublin, the 18th-century home where U2 made the album. Now, all the bassist wants is to share a piece of his 17-acre paradise with his gardener.
He has applied to Dun Laoghaire-Rathdown county council to build a two-bedroom, single-storey cottage that will accommodate the estate’s resident head gardener. Currently that is Darragh Stone, who has worked with the musician for four years. According to documents filed with the planning application, the home will be L-shaped and wrap around a small private courtyard.
It will comprise two bedrooms, a bathroom, utility room, guest lavatory, and an open-plan kitchen and dining area. It will be bigger than the average three-bedroom semi-detached house, measuring 110 sq m.
Clayton has also applied to build new facilities for the maintenance staff who work on his private estate. Along with Stone, there are another four gardeners. The staff building will replace an existing structure and include a gardener’s office, bathroom and kitchen area. The construction will take place in the estate’s 19th-century walled garden.
An existing “deteriorating” glass house will be replaced with a new glass house and potting shed.
Clayton was 28 when he bought Danesmoate, at the foot of the Dublin mountains — the sale was completed in 1988 — and has spent the past 36 years planting the garden.
When he appeared on the BBC’s Gardeners’ World this year, Clayton recalled how he attended boarding school at St Columba’s College nearby in Rathfarnham, and could often be found looking over the wall into Danesmoate, and might even have jumped the wall onto the land. When U2 completed the recording of The Joshua Tree, the album that made them international superstars, the owner of Danesmoate at the time offered to take the price of the rental from the sale price of the house if one of them wanted to buy it.
“I knew whatever happened after The Joshua Tree, I did not want to be walking out my front door onto the street,” Clayton said on the BBC show. He added that at the time he had a “very sketchy knowledge of gardening”.
The grounds sit on a sloping site and the Little Dargle river runs through the property. In the early days Clayton, with the help of a nursery owner nearby, planted about 4,000 trees to mitigate the arrival of the M50, which runs past the property.
Today, the garden has 50 varieties of magnolias, 50 kinds of camellia and 100 varieties of rhododendrons.
In an article on the garden for Country Life last year, the gardening writer Jane Powers said: “Wildlife is abundant at Danesmoate: otters have been spotted, sparrowhawks nest in one of the pines and buzzards are omnipresent.”
On Gardeners’ World, Clayton, who had just returned from a 40-show run at the Sphere in Las Vegas, said that the garden gave him “peace”.
“I didn’t know [when I was buying it] what this would mean to me,” he said. “I didn’t know this would be a place to draw me back and give me such peace.”

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/art/art.title: Behind the scenes with painting SOS
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/art/art.text:
There’s a narrow door set into a passageway of the National Gallery that I must have walked past countless times. Swiped with a security pass, it leads to a warren of corridors and dark staircases. Another door opens and sun floods in through a lantern skylight above the conservation studio. After the cramped backstairs it takes my eyes a moment to adjust. Ahead is Paolo Uccello’s The Battle of San Romano. To my right is the Pollaiuolo brothers’ Martyrdom of Saint Sebastian. Beyond is Parmigianino’s Madonna and Child with Saints. In the next-door studio Cézanne’s Bathers hangs next to Velázquez’s Philip IV of Spain. Paintings that would be separated by centuries in the gallery rooms are here cheek by kingly jowl.
Conservators sit on high tennis-umpire chairs that can be cranked up and down to reach the tops of altarpieces. The largest paintings have their own scaffolding. It feels strangely intimate to see such familiar masterpieces out of their frames, like bursting in on a friend when they are only half-dressed.
Conservation, the cleaning, preservation and occasional repair of works of art, is a constant activity at the National Gallery, but to mark the gallery’s 200th anniversary the conservation studio has redoubled its efforts. The collection is being rehung, ready for a big unveiling next year, and as paintings are moved many of them are sent up here for “treatment”. It may be as simple as surface cleaning to remove accumulated dust and dirt or it may involve more complex work to remove overpaint, discoloured varnish or unsympathetic interventions or to replace lost gilding or address historic damp damage.
The role of the restorer has never been more important. In recent years climate protesters have targeted paintings in landmark European and American museums. The National Gallery has suffered several attacks. Protesters glued themselves to John Constable’s Hay Wain, threw tomato soup at Van Gogh’s Sunflowers and took a hammer to Velázquez’s Venus. Two of the trials are still in progress.
I’m ushered into the office of Larry Keith, the head of conservation at the London gallery. Books line one wall; a series of varnish experiments are pinned to another. We are joined by the conservator Britta New, who has just completed a big conservation project on Rubens’s The Judgment of Paris.
Conservation tends to make the headlines when it’s a botched job. Who can forget the endearingly disastrous “Monkey Christ” perpetrated by the amateur restorer Cecilia Giménez in the church of Santuario de Misericordia in Borja in northeastern Spain? But the professionals approach their paintings with a scrupulous combination of craftsmanship, scholarship and science. “To a pure scientist,” Keith says, “what we’re talking about is pretty basic — what they would call ‘kitchen chemistry’.”
The chemistry may be simple but the application is not. A good conservator needs judgment, an eye for the period they are working on and an understanding of the accretions of history.
“People have different ideas about what good retouching is,” Keith says. “Certainly, 200 years ago most people who restored pictures were effectively painters.” Every restorer is “editing a text” and among Victorian restorers there was a tendency to be more “discursive and broad”.
Before a modern conservator even thinks of picking up a paintbrush, they send the painting to the lab for infrared reflectance imaging spectroscopy and x-ray fluorescence, which can reveal pentimenti (repentances) — changes made by the artist as they refined their composition — and additions by previous restorers. Fig leaves over the naughty bits are a common one.
Only after a report laying out the proposed treatment has been prepared and approved can cleaning begin. First, layers of discoloured varnish are removed. New explains that varnish, often discoloured by years of soot and dust, can leave a “yellowish cast” over the surface. It’s not just that the colours are yellowed, “you’ve actually lost the depth of what you’re looking at, so the darks get lighter, the lights get darker”. In the case of the Rubens, “the whole painting was a little bit flat”.
• Our experts choose their favourite National Gallery paintings
I had assumed that restorers would seek to replicate period pigments. If Rubens used ultramarine, wouldn’t modern restorers grind a new batch of lapis lazuli stones? No, is the answer. The Victorians did use oil paint to retouch paintings, but as Keith explains, the problem with oil paint is that it gets harder and darker as it dries. “Mostly this happens over the first 100 years or so and then that discoloration slows down. So let’s say you are retouching a picture in 1860 that was painted in 1550: you’ve got your 1860 oil paint and you’re whisking it on and you’ve got beautiful colour matching. But the Renaissance painting has stopped darkening. Your retouching may look great now but by the time it comes to us there’s a great blob of darkened mess.”
“We tend to use synthetic pigments,” New explains. “We know they are not going to discolour — they are stable but they are also reversible.” Any paint a National Gallery conservator puts on today goes on top of a layer of varnish so that it can be removed safely in the future without damaging the original paint beneath the varnish. “I could wash it off while I’m talking to you without looking,” Keith says.
“We absolutely replicate old master technique, but we do it on top of our varnish.” They seek to mimic, for example, the opacity or transparency of paint and the density of colour. You can make a purple by layering red and blue or by mixing them. “A colour mix can be much more muddy,” New says. “If you have a beautiful ultramarine underlay and then a red glaze on top of it, you can get the most magical, deep, rich, purple, which you would never get from mixing the two.”
“Our philosophy and that of most museums now,” Keith adds, “is that you should not be able to see our retouchings. They are documented, they’re visible in ultraviolet light. But we don’t really view retouching as performative. We don’t want you to come into the gallery and say, ‘Those clever restorers.’”
For intense, close-up work on, say, a minutely detailed early Netherlandish painting, a restorer might wear optivisors — magnifying lenses on a headband — but a good conservator will always step back and consider the whole. And ideally they work upright. Keith remembers working on a painting so large it couldn’t fit in the studio except on its side. He leans sideways in a Quasimodo crouch to demonstrate how he had to compensate to see it the right way up as he worked. “There were a lot of chiropractors involved.”
The story of the Rubens conservation is a particularly rich one. It wasn’t just that previous restorers had touched-up the original, they had interfered with Rubens’s telling. “It had been completely reworked,” New says. “The story was altered from what Rubens had painted, which was quite a saucy voyeuristic scene in which the three goddesses were stripped of their clothing.”
The Judgment of Paris tells of the moment when Paris is asked to decide who is the fairest: Hera, Aphrodite or Athena, bestowing the winner with a golden apple. Rubens had even painted impatient little putti pulling at the goddesses’ wraps.
• London’s leading contemporary art galleries, ranked
“It was changed into something a lot more modest,” New says. The putti were painted out, as was a lusty satyr in the top corner. Meanwhile, Paris, who in Rubens’s painting held the apple in his lap, lost in contemplation of the goddesses, was repainted to show the moment when he offers the apple. “It becomes the moment of judgment,” Keith says, “rather than the ‘get your kit off’ scene.”
New had the challenge of removing the later paint without damaging the Rubens brushwork below. It wasn’t possible entirely to reveal the putto tugging at Minerva’s wrap, but if you look carefully at the painting returned to Room 18, you can just see the ghost of an impudent hand.
At the National Gallery conservation happens upstairs and out of sight. Recently, the Bowes Museum in Barnard Castle, Co Durham undertook conservation work on one of their Canalettos in the middle of the gallery. Last month visitors would have seen The Regatta on the Grand Canal off the wall and out of its frame as conservators worked to replace the foam that cushions the canvas against its supports, which was beginning to shed black specks.
Jane Whittaker, the principal keeper at the museum, explains that there were two reasons for doing this publicly. One, the museum had noticed the enthusiastic interest visitors took in even the everyday cleaning of paintings and objects. Two, it was too big to fit in the lift. (At the National Gallery, the Saint Sebastian was on its side ready to be trundled out.) It took five people to take the Canaletto off the wall and lower it on to cushioned blocks and two more to stand back and watch for potential hazards and hiccups.
When it comes to cleaning, banish thoughts of yellow dusters and Mr Muscle. Whittaker talks me through the intricacies. Dust can be removed from the tops of frames with a museum vac — a miniature vacuum cleaner with a tiny sable-hair soft brush attachment. Dusting is done with a conservation-grade velvet cloth drawn gently across the surface of the painting. Glass is cleaned with a mild vinegar solution.
Not every gallery has the in-house know-how or studio resources for conservation. Last year Compton Verney in Warwickshire bought a work known as Allegorical Painting of Two Ladies. Painted in the 17th century, it depicts two women, one black and one white, sitting side by side, each wearing equally fine gowns and jewels. The women sport an assortment of curious false “beauty spots” in the form of moons and other symbols. The painting is undergoing conservation at the Yale Centre for British Art in Connecticut.
• Who gets my vote for the worst gallery space in Britain?
Jessica David, the senior paintings conservator at Yale, says it was not in good condition. The varnish was thick and discoloured, at some point it had sustained water damage, leaving drip marks on the surface, and there was a bulge in the canvas where a key had fallen behind the stretcher bar. David’s biggest concern was the dulling of the surface over the hair and face of the black woman on the left.
“All of the darkest shadows in her hair were just completely milky.” Her hair and face had become opaque and all subtlety lost. “You couldn’t see any detail. You couldn’t read her features.”
David first removed a top layer of grime, which is “not uncommon in old paintings that hang in houses with fireplaces”. Then she was faced with several layers of varnish and overpaint. “It was like a sandwich: varnish, restoration, varnish.” As soon as the varnish was off, the “milkiness” vanished. The figure on the left came into focus. “So that was wonderful.”
It was important to restore the flesh tones as sensitively as possible since it is thought that the sitters were deliberately paired to compare their complexions. Research continues into this enigmatic painting, and it will return to Compton Verney at the end of November.
Going back to the changing nature of the job, I ask Keith how he feels when word reaches the conservation studio that a painting has been targeted by protesters. He pauses before saying simply: “It’s never the painting’s fault.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.title: Peace and quiet of Swampy’s eco-village rocked by ‘acid attack’
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.subtitle: Man charged after suspected attack in Tipi Valley, a 200-strong community in Carmarthenshire where Daniel Hooper lives with his family
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/crime/articl.text:
Britain’s largest off-grid community, where the eco-activist Swampy has lived in a turf-roofed roundhouse for the past 20 years, has been rocked by a suspected acid attack.
Police were called to Tipi Valley, a 200-acre expanse of rolling Welsh countryside near Llandeilo, Carmarthenshire, last Wednesday after a resident was injured with a highly corrosive acid.
A manhunt was launched for a suspect from the community by Dyfed-Powys police and 48 hours later Jivan Dean, 23, was arrested.
Dean, of no fixed abode, appeared in Llanelli magistrates’ court on Monday charged with grievous bodily harm and throwing a corrosive substance over a person. He spoke only to confirm his name and date of birth, before being remanded in custody to appear in Swansea crown court next month.
Reported crime is rare at the 100-tent community, which was set up in the mid-1970s by hippies and Christians looking for an off-grid lifestyle.
As Swampy, Daniel Hooper became a household name in 1997 after being the last protester to be taken out of a tunnel built to stop a road-building project in Devon. He later retreated to Tipi Valley, where he started a small forestry enterprise and has brought up three children with his wife Clare.
The community has survived for generations, with more than 100 babies being born there over the years. There are about 200 residents of varying ages, dropping to about 100 in the winter, who are scattered across the secluded valley in tipis, yurts, roundhouses and vans.
• At home with Swampy and son in Tipi Valley
Solar panels power mobile phones and laptops and some residents own cars, while the children are home-schooled or attend local bilingual schools. Visitors are free to stay in the valley, sleeping in Big Lodge, a large tipi erected on a green slope on the edge of the valley.
The community has gradually bought fields from local farmers, with some of the adults working as labourers and teachers around the local villages. Others stay in the valley full time collecting firewood, repairing walkways and tending to crops.
Police said Dean was arrested in the Llanelli area on Friday afternoon after a “vigilant response” from the local community.“We would like to thank all those in our local communities who assisted officers and for their patience and understanding,” they said.
The victim has not been named but locals say they are receiving medical treatment and are under close observation.

image.caption: Tipi Valley was set up in the 1970s by hippies, Christians and people who were looking for an alternative lifestyleALED LLYWELYN/ATHENA
